opening: Alexander Glasgow's documented family begins with Mary/Molly McCaughan and their children in the Rasharkin area. His household, farm succession and probable 1888 Gortahar death provide the foundation for the parentage research. Nancy Glasgow's will, the 1892 probate notice and the Irish household records make Alexander probably Nancy's brother. The shared parent is shown by the Glasgow surname in every branch, so his father was probably John Glasgow, farmer, named in John-867's 1846 marriage. No record names Alexander's own father, and the probate petition remains the decisive test. The Desertoghill identity and the Larne joining generation remain open.

position.answer: Documented Lisnagaver family; confirmed descendant R-FT20271 branch; probable Gortahar death in 1888; father: probably John Glasgow, farmer (Glasgow-4090). This rests on Nancy Glasgow's 1892 heirs citation, the Glasgow birth surname of every sibling branch and John-867's 1846 marriage. It is not directly proved.
points: 1851 census: all five household members transcribed; both spouses report first marriage in 1836.
Six documented children; the 1838 child’s name and the early children’s deaths remain unresolved.
R-FT20271 is confirmed for the tested descendant and James J’s line; their named common ancestor is unknown.
The 1888 Gortahar death is the best-supported located match, with conflicting age and unresolved informant identity.

23 September 2026 evaluation: the 1892 notice serves Alexander's children James, Mary and Ann as heirs, in the same class as the niece and nephew named in Nancy's will, which supports brotherhood. Every sibling branch with a recorded birth surname is Glasgow, pointing to a shared father. John-867's 1846 marriage names him John Glasgow, farmer. The father is therefore probable. Maternity, full/half blood and the Desertoghill identity remain open.
Omissions do not establish exclusions of Thomas, Daniel or the Glenleslie family; completeness, full/half kinship and the applicable property rules still need testing.

17 September 2026 (part 2): Elizabeth (Glasgow) Anderson died at Gortahar 7 Sep 1868 aged 66; Jane Dysart died 13 Sep 1868 aged 64; Ann (Glasgow) McClelland's sons are documented in Bridgeton, Glasgow; James Dysart's 1881 will names granddaughter Mary Anne McCaughern, who witnessed John-867's daughter's 1875 wedding. A Daniel Glasgow (c.1817–1867) died at Culmore. No record yet names Alexander's own father.
Larne is a priority origin hypothesis: compare James-1509 as Adam’s father and the older-Alexander or younger-James routes to Alexander; test Robert under Archibald on the American side.

evidence_questions.title: What establishes Alexander’s identity and approximate dates?
evidence_questions.answer: The original 1851 Lisnagaver census establishes the household. The 1888 Gortahar death remains its best-supported later-life match; the named alternative at Glenleslie has a weaker fit.
evidence_questions.reasoning: The five-person 1851 household, father-naming marriages, exact lot-25 succession to Robert Elder, and Mary Elder’s appearance at her mother’s Gortahar death connect family and locality. Ann’s 1876 marriage also calls Alexander a labourer. The death’s age conflicts and daughter Nancy is not yet identified.
evidence_questions.limitation: The tithe and valuation entries name occupiers but do not identify an age or prove that every entry is the same Alexander. The 1888 age implies an earlier birth than the census.
evidence_questions.missing: An original record linking the 1851 farmer to the Gortahar death, or a record resolving the conflicting ages and informant relationship.

evidence_questions.title: Which records establish his partner and children?
evidence_questions.answer: Rasharkin baptisms, the 1851 household and later civil marriages form a coherent family with Mary/Molly McCaughan. They do not justify merging the two James profiles or supplying a name for the 1838 child.
evidence_questions.reasoning: The baptism entries name Alex/Alexander and Mary/Molly at Gortereagh and Lisnagaver; the census places Mary and several children in one household; later marriages independently name Alexander as father of Robert, Mary and Ann.
evidence_questions.limitation: The marriage of Alexander and Mary has not been located. The 1838 transcription is unnamed, and the first James may have died before the reused name appears in 1843. Tree attachment alone does not establish every relationship.
evidence_questions.missing: An onsite or ordered copy of the original 1838 baptism page, the marriage or session record for Alexander and Mary, and records explaining the first James and unnamed child.

evidence_questions.title: What is actually known about his parents?
evidence_questions.answer: No inspected contemporary record names Alexander’s parents. Older Alexander and Rosanna remain the maintained working hypothesis, while the imported Robert/Catherine attachment is not established.

related_question.label: Thomas–Daniel proof: will, marriage and the missing Alexander link

evidence_questions.reasoning: The late tradition gives a specific proposed parent pair for Thomas and the local records place Alexander near Thomas and Daniel. That makes the hypothesis worth testing, but locality and a later tradition do not supply Alexander’s missing parentage link.
evidence_questions.limitation: The only further provenance found is a 2018 FamilySearch Pedigree Resource File citing an Ancestry member tree; it gives a conflicting Rosanna death date and no historical source. The 1834 occupiers and later neighbouring farms do not state kinship; the John Glasgow Bible family is a nearby comparison, not a proved alternative parentage.
evidence_questions.missing: Kilraughts family or society material, the source provenance for Rosanna’s name and death date, or another contemporary record naming Alexander’s father or parents.

evidence_questions.title: How is Alexander connected to Thomas and Daniel?
evidence_questions.answer: Daniel’s will identifies Thomas as his brother, and Daniel Neely Glasgow’s marriage identifies Thomas as his father. This establishes the Thomas–Daniel family network, not Alexander’s relationship to it.
evidence_questions.reasoning: Daniel’s will calls Thomas his late brother and names nephew Daniel Neely Glasgow. The 1888 marriage identifies Daniel Neely as the son of Thomas, a farmer, and connects him to Lisnagaver. The distinctive full name, father’s name and local family context identify the nephew with Thomas’s son; this is more than two occurrences of the common name Thomas. That chain identifies the relevant Thomas and establishes Daniel’s brotherhood. Neither record names Alexander as their brother or identifies the brothers’ parents.
evidence_questions.limitation: Neither record calls Alexander a brother. The correspondence is a private, public-safe summary of a reported autosomal match; match metrics, pedigree and the source behind the parent names remain unavailable.
evidence_questions.missing: The underlying match data and pedigree, the original source for the parent tradition, and a record explicitly connecting Alexander to Thomas or Daniel.

evidence_questions.title: What does the DNA evidence add, and what does it leave unresolved?
evidence_questions.answer: The tested Alexander-descendant line and the tested James J Glasgow line both belong to R-FT20271. This confirms shared paternal ancestry; their named common ancestor and exact relationship remain unknown.
evidence_questions.reasoning: The public FTDNA project confirms Big Y-700/R-FT20271 for both lines. The maintained Y-111 comparison reports genetic distance three. This is an established result, distinct from the unverified autosomal lead to Thomas’s descendants.
evidence_questions.limitation: Neither the shared SNP nor STR distance identifies a father or a cousin degree. No exclusive downstream named SNP for just these two lines appears in the inspected Block Tree.
evidence_questions.missing: Documentary links above both confirmed ancestors and independent descendant-branch comparisons.

census-1851.recorded_statement: House 35: Alexander 40, farmer, reads/writes; Mary 40, reads; both Antrim-born, married in 1836; Robert 10 and James 7, sons at school; Ann 4, daughter. All five give Antrim birthplaces.
census-1851.relevance: The combination of age, birthplace, occupation, residence and household makes this the principal identity anchor for the later records.
census-1851.limitation: The return does not name his parents, and it does not by itself prove that every later Alexander Glasgow entry is the same man.

death-alexander-1888.recorded_statement: Entry 348: 16 May 1888, Gortahar; Alexander Glasgow, married labourer, 84; gangrene for three months; Nancy Glasgow, daughter, present at death, of Gortahar; registered 25 May.
death-alexander-1888.relevance: The Elder/Glasgow family bridge to Gortahar and Ann’s father-naming 1876 marriage make this the best-supported located identification.
death-alexander-1888.limitation: The age implies c.1804 rather than census-derived c.1811. Nancy is not securely identified; the register names no wife or previous address.

tithe-1834.recorded_statement: The tithe entry names Alexr Glasgow as occupier of 29 acres at Lisnagaver in 1834.
tithe-1834.relevance: It places a Glasgow occupier of the right name in the locality before the family baptisms and census.
tithe-1834.limitation: No age, residence, kinship or identifying detail connects this occupier conclusively to the man in the 1851 census.

valuation-1863-1878.recorded_statement: The valuation revision books continue Alexander Glasgow on Lisnagaver lot 25 beside John and Thomas Glasgow during the 1863–1878 volume.
valuation-1863-1878.relevance: The continuing lot number supports tenancy continuity for the Lisnagaver Alexander and his local context.
valuation-1863-1878.limitation: A valuation entry can lag a change in occupation and does not establish a precise death date, parentage or sibling relationship.

baptism-james-1837.recorded_statement: Entry 75 records Jas Glascaw, born 17 January 1837 and baptised 9 February 1837, father Alex, mother Mary McAughin, residence Gortereagh.
baptism-james-1837.relevance: The birth date identifies the early James. The parents’ names and locality contribute to the continuing family sequence.
baptism-james-1837.limitation: The source is a transcription. Identifying these adults with the later Lisnagaver couple depends on the combined baptism and household evidence, not this entry alone.

baptism-unnamed-1838.recorded_statement: Rasharkin entry 106 names Alex and Molly McAughern as parents of an unnamed Glasgow child at Gortereagh in 1838.
baptism-unnamed-1838.relevance: It is the concrete record behind the preserved unnamed-child relationship.
baptism-unnamed-1838.limitation: The published entry preserves neither a forename nor a precise baptism date, and no free original image was found. MIC1P/292 requires onsite inspection or an ordered page copy, so the child must not be merged with either James.

baptism-james-1843.recorded_statement: Rasharkin entry 203 records James, born 9 October 1843 at Lisnagaver, as the child of Alex and Molly McAughern; the baptism was entered on 7 January 1844.
baptism-james-1843.relevance: The place, parents and date identify the later James as a distinct child in the continuing household.
baptism-james-1843.limitation: The reused name and the separate 1837 entry prevent treating this as the same James without the maintained identity assessment.

census-1851.recorded_statement: The 1851 Lisnagaver household includes Alexander, Mary and children Robert, James and Ann.
census-1851.relevance: It links the couple and the named children in one household and supplies continuity from the baptism records.
census-1851.limitation: It does not record a marriage date, and absence from a household cannot alone resolve the first James or unnamed 1838 child.

marriage-robert-1866.recorded_statement: Robert Glasgow named Alexander Glasgow, farmer, as his father in the 5 April 1866 marriage return.
marriage-robert-1866.relevance: This is a direct later father statement supporting Robert as Alexander’s child.
marriage-robert-1866.limitation: The return does not state Alexander’s age or prove the exact birth date imported for Robert.

marriage-mary-1871.recorded_statement: Mary Glasgow of Lisnagaver named Alexander Glasgow, farmer, as her father in the 14 June 1871 marriage return.
marriage-mary-1871.relevance: It independently identifies Mary’s father and preserves her Lisnagaver connection.
marriage-mary-1871.limitation: It does not name Mary’s mother or establish that every child attached in the tree belonged to the same marriage.

marriage-ann-1876.recorded_statement: Ann Glasgow named Alexander Glasgow, labourer, as her father in the 13 October 1876 marriage return and was associated with Lisnagaver.
marriage-ann-1876.relevance: It supplies a direct father statement for Ann and extends the family identification beyond the 1851 census.
marriage-ann-1876.limitation: The different occupation wording and lack of a mother’s name leave the household bridge indirect.

will-daniel-1871.recorded_statement: Daniel Glasgow’s will calls Thomas Glasgow his late brother and Daniel Neely Glasgow his nephew.
will-daniel-1871.relevance: It directly establishes Daniel and Thomas as brothers and provides the nephew identity needed to identify the relevant Thomas family.
will-daniel-1871.limitation: It does not name Alexander, the parents of the brothers or the degree of Alexander’s relationship to them.

marriage-daniel-neely-1888.recorded_statement: Daniel Neely Glasgow’s 28 June 1888 marriage return names Thomas Glasgow, farmer, as his father.
marriage-daniel-neely-1888.relevance: The full son’s name connects the Thomas named in the will to the Lisnagaver Thomas family rather than relying on a shared surname.
marriage-daniel-neely-1888.limitation: The return identifies Thomas as Daniel Neely’s father but does not identify Alexander as Thomas’s brother or son of the proposed older pair.

tithe-1834.recorded_statement: An Alexr Glasgow occupied Lisnagaver in 1834, where later records also place the Thomas–Daniel network.
tithe-1834.relevance: It supplies locality context for the working hypothesis that the families may be closely related.
tithe-1834.limitation: Neighbouring or repeated Glasgow occupations are not a parent or sibling statement, and the occupier’s identity is not independently resolved.

will-daniel-1871.recorded_statement: Daniel’s will identifies Thomas as his brother and Daniel Neely Glasgow as his nephew.
will-daniel-1871.relevance: This is the sibling half of the identity bridge and is separate from the later marriage evidence.
will-daniel-1871.limitation: The will stops at Daniel’s relationship to Thomas; Alexander is not mentioned as a brother.

marriage-daniel-neely-1888.recorded_statement: The marriage return records Daniel Neely Glasgow and names Thomas Glasgow as his father.
marriage-daniel-neely-1888.relevance: This is the father-and-son half of the bridge, matching the nephew named in Daniel’s will to Thomas’s son.
marriage-daniel-neely-1888.limitation: It does not state how Alexander is related to Thomas or Daniel, so the network cannot be extended to brotherhood from these records alone.

census-1851.recorded_statement: Alexander headed a Lisnagaver household in 1851, in the same local area as the Thomas family records.
census-1851.relevance: It provides contemporary locality context for testing a close relationship.
census-1851.limitation: Enumeration proximity is not a kinship statement and cannot replace the will or marriage identity bridge.

correspondence-thomas-2020.recorded_statement: A public-safe summary of February 2020 correspondence reports an autosomal match and a descendant line from Thomas, alongside an Alexander-and-Rosanna tradition.
correspondence-thomas-2020.relevance: It gives a concrete descendant and DNA route for testing Alexander’s connection to Thomas’s branch.
correspondence-thomas-2020.limitation: The underlying match metrics, pedigree, message provenance and source for the parent names are not published or independently verified.

correspondence-thomas-2020.recorded_statement: The correspondence summary reports a match with a descendant of Thomas and a belief that Thomas’s parents were Alexander and Rosanna.
correspondence-thomas-2020.relevance: It is an actionable autosomal lead directed at the exact unresolved bridge in the parent hypothesis.
correspondence-thomas-2020.limitation: A reported match without shared-DNA metrics, segments and a complete pedigree cannot distinguish brothers, cousins or an alternative shared line.

biography_sections.title: Alexander’s life in its local setting
biography_sections.markdown:
Alexander’s records describe a family rooted in a small part of County Antrim, with children whose later lives lead beyond it. His clearest surviving household is at Lisnagaver in 1851: an Antrim-born farmer, his wife Mary, and three children. Earlier baptisms recover the beginnings of that family; later marriages and the Elder tenancy connect it to the next generation. The probable Gortahar death completes the broad outline, with the last identity link still open.

### The places in his life

{{figure:places.svg}}

[Gortereghy](https://www.townlands.ie/en/antrim/kilconway/rasharkin/killoquin-upper/gortereghy/), written Gortereagh in the baptism transcription, adjoins [Lisnagaver](https://www.townlands.ie/en/antrim/kilconway/rasharkin/killoquin/lisnagaver/) to the south. [Gortahar](https://www.townlands.ie/antrim/kilconway/rasharkin/killoquin/gortahar/) lies northeast, beyond Moneyleck. They are distinct townlands within the same parish. The map shows approximate modern townland locations, not reconstructed houses or field boundaries.

Both spouses reported first marriage in 1836. Their children’s baptisms place them at Gortereagh in 1837–38 and Lisnagaver by 1843. That suggests a change in the family’s recorded residence between neighbouring townlands; it does not date a move precisely or establish a return to a paternal home. Mary’s possible local family connections deserve investigation in their own right.

The census’s farmer and literate household, the small assessed tenancy and the children’s marriages recover part of Alexander’s circumstances. Later records call him a labourer, and his son-in-law succeeds him on the holding. These changes are compatible with an altered working role as he aged, but their cause is unknown. No inspected source establishes eviction, poverty, or illness-induced retirement. The [record sequence and farm analysis](#record-account) distinguish those observations from assumptions about his life.

The following account traces marriage and children, examines the surviving household, then follows the farm, probable death and paternal connections. Missing parentage is one question within that family history.

biography_sections.title: Marriage, Mary’s family and the children
biography_sections.markdown:
Alexander Glasgow and Mary/Molly McCaughan are a documented couple. Their [1851 household](#census-household) reports first marriage in 1836, but no original marriage entry has been located. Rasharkin Presbyterian’s surviving marriage register begins in 1845; First Kilraughts material (Coleraine Family History Society film 197, marriages from 1831) remains a focused alternative.

The marriage-year statement fits the first directly located record sequence. The published transcription of the original Rasharkin Presbyterian register, PRONI `MIC1P/292`, records the same parental couple at Gortereagh: James Glascaw was born 17 January and baptised 9 February 1837 to Alex and Mary McAughin; an incomplete 1838 entry records a Glascow child of Alex and Molly McAughern; and a later James Glascow was born 9 October 1843 and baptised 7 January 1844 to Alex and Molly McAughern at Lisnagaver. The named transcription can be checked at [Rasharkin Presbyterian baptisms](https://genealogy.torrens.org/BannValley/church/RasharkinP/Baptisms_1834.html). The register transcription preserves Mary/Molly and McAughin/McAughern. The repeated parental names and residences support their identification with Mary McCaughan while retaining the spellings actually recorded.

The Gortereagh residence is meaningful maternal context, but it is not a parentage proof. The 1834 tithe list includes William and James McCaheran there, a spelling compatible with the recorded McAughin/McAughern/McCaughan forms. This makes a McCaughan family connection a reasonable explanation to test for the newly married couple’s residence, perhaps through Mary's people or a subtenancy. It does not prove that either man was Mary's father, nor that the first son James was named for a maternal grandfather. The 1851 Lisnagaver evidence supplies a more concrete lead: Mary McCaheren, 22, lived with farmer Archibald McCaheren, 60, and Elizabeth in house 31. She is the strongest currently located candidate for the later 1855 bride who named her father as Archy, but that is a separate McCaughan problem. It does not establish Mary Glasgow’s parentage. Likewise, the household of widowed Sarah McCaghrin and grandchildren beside widowed Margaret Elder and children is evidence of a local network of families and neighbours, not an expressed kinship.

The Gortereagh names are recorded in the 1834 Rasharkin tithe book, PRONI **FIN/5/A/236**; the 1851 McCaheren and Elder groupings are in Lisnagaver houses 31 and 5. These are separate record observations, not confirmed maternal relatives. See the [National Archives census collection](https://nationalarchives.ie/collections/search-the-census/) and [PRONI tithe-book guide](https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/articles/tithe-applotment-books).

### Six children, with different kinds of evidence


| Child | Dates supported by records | Evidence and what remains uncertain |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [James Glasgow (Glasgow-3939)](/people/glasgow-3939.html) | Born 17 January 1837; baptised 9 February | Rasharkin entry 75 names Alex and Mary McAughin at Gortereagh. Reuse of James in 1843 suggests this child died young; no death or burial has been found. |
| [Unnamed Glasgow child (Glasgow-3940)](/people/glasgow-3940.html) | Entry in the 1838 baptism sequence | Entry 106 names Alex and Molly McAughern at Gortereagh. The parent relationship is documented; the forename and precise birth/baptism dates are not preserved in the transcription. No death date is proved. |
| [Robert Glasgow (Glasgow-938)](/people/glasgow-938.html) | Born about 1840–41 | Aged 10 in 1851 and 25 at his 1866 marriage. Both records name Alexander as father. The imported exact date 6 November 1840 has no identified supporting record. |
| [Mary Glasgow, later Elder (Glasgow-3167)](/people/glasgow-3167.html) | Aged 28 at marriage in 1871; birth year uncertain | Her marriage names Alexander Glasgow, farmer, and gives Lisnagaver residence. Husband Robert Elder’s later occupation of Alexander’s lot and her role at her mother’s 1892 death strengthen the family identification. She is not listed in house 35 in 1851. |
| [James Glasgow (Glasgow-973)](/people/glasgow-973.html) | Born 9 October 1843; baptised 7 January 1844 | Rasharkin entry 203 names Alex and Molly McAughern at Lisnagaver. The seven-year-old son in 1851 fits this child. His later life remains under investigation. |
| [Ann Glasgow, later McCracken (Glasgow-438)](/people/glasgow-438.html) | Born about 1846–47; married 13 October 1876 | Four-year-old daughter in 1851; her 1876 marriage independently names Alexander Glasgow, labourer. Her identity with the 1888 informant Nancy is possible but unproved. |

Sources: [Rasharkin Presbyterian baptism transcription, entries 75, 106 and 203](https://genealogy.torrens.org/BannValley/church/RasharkinP/Baptisms_1834.html), from PRONI **MIC1P/292**; [1851 household image](https://nationalarchives.ie/collections/search-the-census/view-pdf/?doc=007246523_00175&c19=true); the civil marriages linked in the record table below. The baptism evidence is a named transcription; the original incomplete 1838 entry still needs inspection. The two James entries represent separate children, not a duplicate caused by a date discrepancy.

### What the gaps mean

The early children are documented separately from their inferred deaths. The table’s reuse-of-name argument does not supply an exact death date. Nor does the incomplete 1838 transcription identify its child as Samuel: an original copy of **MIC1P/292, entry 106** is needed to read the missing name and dates.

The transcription has no entries for 1840 or 1841, around Robert’s likely birth. Failure to find his baptism in that transcription is therefore weak evidence against the known parentage: the census and marriage positively establish his father. The missing original marriage, incomplete baptism entry and missing burial records are different gaps and need different searches.

The unnamed child would have been about twelve or thirteen in 1851. No resident, absent-person or household-death entry records that child in the maintained return audit. That omission weighs against an uncomplicated survival-and-emigration reconstruction, but cannot fix a death date or guarantee that the return was complete. The candidate Samuel Glasgow in Michigan was rejected because no American record supplied the required Antrim/parent bridge and the proposal also had to explain this omission. An impossible February date in a later cemetery transcription cannot name the child. The [child’s assessment](/people/glasgow-3940.html) preserves the comparison.

reading_summary.question: Who were Mary and the children?
reading_summary.finding: The couple and six children are documented; Mary’s parents, the 1838 child’s name and early deaths remain unresolved.

biography_sections.title: Mary’s parentage research: new findings and limits
biography_sections.markdown:
The current evidence does **not** prove the parents of [Mary (McCaughan) Glasgow](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/McCaughan-222). The complete 1851 Rasharkin-derived return contains several distinct McCaheren/McCaughern/McCaghrin households, including Mary McCaheren, age 70, as Margaret Taylor’s mother-in-law; none identifies Mary Glasgow or names her parents. The Rasharkin baptism transcription separately records Eliza McAughern with Thomas, Archy McAughern with Elizabeth Kilpatrick, and James McAughern with John and Jane McAuly. These establish a local network, not one merged family.

Other documented candidate clusters include William and James McCaheran at Gortereghy; Alexr. McCaughan at Unchenagh in Finvoy; and John McCaughey/McCahan at Drumadarragh. The National Archives census-search-form database adds a later Gortahar family: Thomas McCaughern/McCaughan, son of John McCaughern and Mary Gormley. None is directly connected to Mary Glasgow.

Authenticated FamilySearch searches for Mary McCaughan, McAughin, McAughern and McCaheren in the relevant period returned no indexed result. The apparent Alexander–Mary McCaughan hits are a different Catholic Culfeightrin/Ballycastle family, including Mary M’caughan’s 7 April 1867 baptism to Alex M’caughan and Cath Quinn. A Mary McCaughern–William Marks cluster is later and unrelated.

The strongest unresolved route is the pre-1831 **Kilraughts–Dervock Reformed Presbyterian society material**, PRONI `CR5/32A/1` and related catalogue references `CR5/32/1/1/1–2`. The guide describes member-by-society lists, baptisms, marriages, deaths, removals and emigrations from about 1804–1831. Since Mary was probably born about 1811, a household entry could name her parents. Kilraughts and Dervock operated together until their 1831 division, so both contexts must be searched. The manuscript has not been inspected; this is a high-priority evidence target, not proof.

Sources: [Rasharkin Presbyterian baptism transcription](https://genealogy.torrens.org/BannValley/church/RasharkinP/Baptisms_1834.html); [North Antrim tithe material](https://www.billmacafee.com/182030stithe/tithenorthantrimrevisionorder.pdf); [Ulster Lees Ballymoney study](https://ulsterlees.azurewebsites.net/families/co-antrim/ballymoney-area/); [FamilySearch search](https://www.familysearch.org/en/search/record/results?count=100&q.givenName=Mary&q.surname=McAughern&q.birthLikeDate.from=1780&q.birthLikeDate.to=1840&q.birthLikePlace=Antrim%2C%20Ireland); [PRONI Guide to Church Records](https://www.americanancestors.org/sites/default/files/2026-03/Guide-to-Church-Records-October-2019.pdf); [RootsIreland County Antrim sources](https://rootsireland.ie/antrimdown/online-sources.php); [Ballymoney church history](https://eddiesextracts.com/books/churchesofballymoney/reformedchurch.html).

reading_summary.question: What new evidence bears on Mary’s parents?
reading_summary.finding: The local surname clusters are now separated, but no parent link is proved; the Kilraughts–Dervock society lists are the highest-value unresolved source.
reading_summary.purpose: Consolidates the new evidence and preserves the proof boundary.

biography_sections.title: Mary Anne M‘Caughern witness in the John Glasgow family
biography_sections.markdown:
At Finvoy Parish Church on 18 February 1875, [Ann Glasgow](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Glasgow-1371), daughter of [John Glasgow](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Glasgow-867), married Francis Bellingham ([marriage note](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/McCaughan-222#_note-BellinghamGlasgow1875)). The witnesses were Thomas Bellingham and **Mary Anne M‘Caughern**. This is a useful record-level link between John’s Glasgow family and the McCaughern network around Lisnagaver.

The witness remains unidentified. The register says Mary Anne rather than Mary/Molly, uses a different surname spelling, and does not establish that Alexander’s wife was living in 1875. Other McCaughan/McAughern households existed locally. This supports a cautious network observation, not an identification of Mary Anne with Alexander’s wife or proof that Alexander and John were related.

reading_summary.question: Does John’s family share the McCaughern network?
reading_summary.finding: A Mary Anne M‘Caughern witnessed a John Glasgow family marriage in 1875; her identity and relationship to Alexander’s wife remain unproved.
reading_summary.purpose: Records a useful local-network link without collapsing distinct women or families.

biography_sections.title: The Black branch and Robert’s possible witness
biography_sections.markdown:
The original [5 April 1866 marriage return](https://civilrecords.irishgenealogy.ie/churchrecords/images/marriage_returns/marriages_1866/11531/8240963.pdf) for Robert Glasgow and Jane Graham names Robert’s father as Alexander Glasgow, farmer, and records **John Black** as a witness. The return gives no address or relationship, so the witness identity is not settled.

A specific candidate emerges from the Canadian deed research. The [13 March 1862 marriage return](https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/marriage_returns/marriages_1862/10945/5491449.pdf) identifies John Black of Drumoolish as a full-age bachelor, farmer, son of **Robert Black**, farmer; Martha Savage, 20, was of Knockaduff and daughter of William Savage. The names, townland and farming context make this a strong identity anchor for the deed’s John and Martha.

The Churchtown [baptism transcription](https://genealogy.torrens.org/BannValley/church/TamlaghtP/Baptisms.html) records **Elizabeth Black**, 31 July 1845, daughter of **Robert Black and Mary Glasgow**, resident Drumoolish (page 7, entry 116; PRONI MIC 1P/347A/1). This supplies a named parental couple for the Black branch, but the original image remains unchecked and 31 July is a baptism date, not an established birth date. The same transcription has “Thomson Black,” 10 January 1843, with mother transcribed “Gear” and marked illegible; it must not be changed to Thomasina without the image.

The [1831 census transcription](https://genealogy.torrens.org/BannValley/church/Tamlaght/1831census_2.html) lists Robert Black at Drumolish, house 57, with two males and one female, but the occupants are unnamed and several Black households occur in the townland. The [December 1862 report](https://www.cotyroneireland.com/surnames/black3.html) and [5 November 1863 baptisms](https://genealogy.torrens.org/BannValley/church/TamlaghtP/Baptisms2.html) support continuity for John and Martha’s family, although the reported 20 December birth and nine-month baptism age conflict.

**Assessment:** the 1866 witness is established; identifying him as the John Black, son of Robert Black and Mary Glasgow, is plausible but unproved. Even if confirmed, it would show contact with Alexander’s son, not shared parentage or brotherhood. Obtain the Elizabeth and 1843 baptism images, investigate Robert Black and Mary Glasgow’s marriage and household, and compare further Churchtown witness occurrences before drawing a kinship conclusion.

reading_summary.question: Who was John Black at Robert’s marriage?
reading_summary.finding: A Drumoolish John Black is a plausible witness identification, and Robert Black with Mary Glasgow is a named parental couple; neither link is proved to Alexander’s parentage.
reading_summary.purpose: Adds the new collateral route while separating a recorded witness from an inferred identity.

biography_sections.title: 1892 New York probate notice: Mary and Ann named as Alexander’s children
biography_sections.markdown:
Nancy Glasgow's [will](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:33SQ-GYC4-66V?view=fullText) and the [23 January 1892 probate notice](https://fultonhistory.com/Newspaper%2024/Plattsburg%20NY%20Republican/Plattsburg%20NY%20Republican%201889-1892/Plattsburg%20NY%20Republican%201889-1892%20-%201042.pdf) connect the Irish Glasgow, Dysart and Anderson households. The notice names James, Mary and Ann as children of Alexander formerly of Rasharkin. Their identification with this family is probable, supported by the separate Lisnagaver marriage/baptism records. Nancy's will names Margaret Kennedy as niece and Robert Anderson as nephew. The complete notice has now been inspected; the earlier OCR-only limitation is superseded.

**Relationship assessment, 21 September 2026.** The will and citation favour a probable sibling network; they do not name Alexander's father or prove full rather than half siblinghood. Elizabeth Anderson is identified through the baptism evidence, not named as a parent in the notice. John-867's recorded father is a conditional candidate; his identity with the Desertoghill flax grower is another unproved step.

Omission of Thomas's descendants does not exclude Thomas or Daniel. The notes themselves raise an omitted possible nephew, Robert-938, whose later Scottish identity/survival needs verification. Residence of Daniel Neely somewhere in New York does not establish the informant's knowledge. The notice concerns real and personal property: [Matter of De Voe](https://law.justia.com/cases/new-york/appellate-division/1905/107-ad-245.html) distinguishes their representation rules. Inspect Nancy's petition, heir schedule, amendments and service papers before interpreting the notice as an exhaustive pedigree.

reading_summary.question: What does Nancy's probate establish about Alexander's family?
reading_summary.finding: The inspected notice, will and Irish household records support a probable sibling network; common fatherhood and completeness remain unproved.
reading_summary.purpose: Separates positive kinship evidence from unsupported exclusions and identifies the missing probate papers.

biography_sections.title: Following the children into adult life
biography_sections.markdown:
### Robert: the recorded son and the Scottish continuation

Robert, aged ten in 1851, is directly recorded as Alexander and Mary’s son in the same Lisnagaver household. His [5 April 1866 marriage to Jane Graham](https://civilrecords.irishgenealogy.ie/churchrecords/images/marriage_returns/marriages_1866/11531/8240963.pdf) independently calls him a Lisnagaver farmer and names his father Alexander Glasgow, farmer. Those two records make Robert `Glasgow-938` the documented child, with estimated birth about 1840–41 from the census and marriage ages. The often repeated exact 6 November 1840 birth date has no identified supporting original. His probable identification with a later Gortereghy valuation occupier is useful local continuity, but that identification is separate from the proved father–son relationship.

Robert’s later family is followed into Glasgow, Scotland, in the maintained account, which cites a [1871 Scottish census index for Robert](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:QV9Y-71S6) and an [1881 index for the younger Alexander](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:VQQ8-5MB). [Alexander Glasgow (Glasgow-937)](/people/glasgow-937.html), born about 1871, is the next historical generation in that family reconstruction. The Irish census and marriage provide the direct father–son argument for Alexander-951 and Robert; the Scottish continuation relies here on the maintained census references, not newly inspected original images. The copied exact birth date for the younger Alexander had been cited to the same index used for the census, so it is not adopted as an independently verified birth in this account. Exact Scottish address chronology and Robert’s reported 1902 death remain checks on their own originals.

This carries the story beyond the Antrim farm without making every copied detail equally secure. The tested descendant’s confirmed paternal ancestry reaches Alexander-951; the [Y-DNA section](#paternal-dna) explains the genetic comparison without listing living generations.

{{record:robert1866-marriage}}

The precise Scottish birth-image leads and the misplaced 1902 death citation are assessed in the [next research tests](#next-research). Neither has yet been inspected; the direct Irish father–son evidence remains secure.

### James: a strong Michigan candidate, still an open identity

The second James, `Glasgow-973`, has an unusually clear Irish identity: the 1843–44 baptism and his age seven appearance in the 1851 household establish him as Alexander and Mary’s child. His subsequent association with the James Glasgow buried at Tecumseh, Michigan is strong but still unproved. The Michigan household is well reconstructed: [the original 1884 Michigan census image](https://michigan.access.preservica.com/uncategorized/IO_eb4d3f94-3c2f-4701-b5bb-c3ecee9ef9b9/) gives a forty-year-old Irish-born baggage agent, and the Brookside register identifies the associated wife and daughters. His daughter Minnie’s [1941 death certificate](https://michigan.access.preservica.com/uncategorized/IO_3dab599e-1093-473c-be85-eee5e9b49154/) reports James as born in County Antrim. That narrows the comparison materially but names neither Alexander nor Mary and gives no Lisnagaver detail. The 1869 original marriage return, naturalisation papers, or a passenger record is still required before the Michigan life becomes Alexander’s son’s biography.

### Ann: a later marriage and the Nancy problem

Ann, `Glasgow-438`, is likewise direct family evidence. She was aged four in 1851 and her [13 October 1876 marriage to Robert McCracken](https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/marriage_returns/marriages_1876/11181/8097170.pdf) calls her a full-age spinster of Lisnagaver and names Alexander Glasgow, labourer, as father. The occupational wording matters because it independently makes the 1888 Gortahar death’s “labourer” compatible with the former Lisnagaver farmer; it is not grounds to split the two men. Ann’s later married surname also means Nancy Glasgow, who reported Alexander’s 1888 death, cannot simply be equated with her. A separate daughter, or another explanation, remains possible.

{{record:ann1876-marriage}}

### Mary: the daughter whose records connect the households

Mary `Glasgow-3167` is not in the 1851 return but is securely added by her [14 June 1871 marriage to Robert Elder](https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/marriage_returns/marriages_1871/11341/8162804.pdf): aged 28, resident Lisnagaver, she named Alexander Glasgow, farmer, as father. Her marriage, Robert Elder’s succession to lot 25, and the Gortahar deaths create the high-confidence bridge between the Lisnagaver couple and Mary McCaughan’s later identity. Mary Glasgow’s [17 February 1892 death return](https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/deaths_returns/deaths_1892/06049/4723532.pdf) records daughter Mary Elder as informant. It does not state a maiden surname or husband, and its reported age 89 conflicts with the retained c.1811 estimate; those limits belong beside the identification, not beneath it.

Mary’s later household also contains an instructive name conflict. Her granddaughter’s [1908 birth](https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/birth_returns/births_1908/01647/1657700.pdf) records **Samuel Elder**, son of Jane Elder, with no father named; the [1911 household](https://nationalarchives.ie/collections/search-the-census/census-record/#id=490671&c20_year=1911) calls him **Samuel Glasgow**. The surname is genuinely present in the census, not merely a modern transcription mistake. These records help reconstruct the continuing family, but neither identifies his father. It would be circular to invent a Glasgow father and then use that invented relationship to strengthen Alexander’s ancestry.

Mary’s absence in 1851 is consequently an unresolved location question within a well-supported later family identification. It does not erase the 1871 father statement. Nor does it establish that she was the Maryan in John of Glenleslie’s household: the roughly nine-year conflict between their implied birth years requires explanation, and no located record joins those two identities.

reading_summary.finding: Adult records extend the family; James’s Michigan identity and Ann’s identification as Nancy remain unresolved.
reading_summary.purpose: Separates established parentage from later identity matches.

The register does not name Mary’s deceased husband. |

### The reported 1829 occurrence: an age and identity test

The original newspaper alert of **12 September 2025** was inspected directly on 13 September 2026. Its [MyHeritage result, 12021-100828509](https://www.myheritage.com/research/record-12021-100828509-/alexander-glasgow-in-united-kingdom-names-stories-in-newspapers-from-oldnewscom), does quote **“Alex. Glasgow, Lisnagaver”** from the **Belfast News-Letter, 5 June 1829**. The [British Newspaper Archive issue index](https://www.britishnewspaperarchive.com/image-viewer?issue=BL%2F0000038%2F18290605&page=0004&article=015) independently locates the Lisnagaver entry in **page 4, article 015**. Its OCR mangles Glasgow, explaining why a surname search missed the article while a townland search found it. These are two derivative extracts of one newspaper occurrence, not two independent historical records.

The archive’s damaged heading excerpt appears to concern persons applying to register, with special sessions at Ballymoney, under **County of Antrim**. That makes a registration notice the specific working context, but the full image and governing columns remain unread: MyHeritage now presents a subscription paywall and the archive viewer requires sign-in. The extract cannot yet establish an adult qualification, successful registration or the man’s identity. The earlier claim that even the alert was uninspected is superseded; the historical interpretation remains open.

| Identity being tested | Approximate age on 5 June 1829 | What the original could distinguish |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Alexander-951 using the 1851 census age | About 18 | A general subscription, petition or resident list might accommodate him. An entry requiring a particular adult qualification would need that requirement and its date checked. |
| Alexander-951 using the probable 1888 death age | About 25 | Fits an adult occurrence more comfortably, but depends on both the death identification and the reported death age being correct. |
| An older Alexander, possibly the man represented by [Glasgow-3904](/people/glasgow-3904.html) | About 59 if the estimated 1770 birth is used | A senior/junior label, occupation, related party or other identifying detail might support an older namesake. Name and townland alone do not establish one. |

The important distinction is between **an older birth date for the same man** and **a second, older man**. Even if the notice proves adult status, it would not automatically make the subject Alexander's father. Conversely, identifying the subject from the 1888 age and then using him to validate that same death identification would be circular. No birth estimate or parent ranking changes on the extract alone.

If the subject is Alexander-951, the occurrence would support a premarital Lisnagaver association before the couple's Gortereagh baptisms of 1837–38 and their documented Lisnagaver residence by 1843. That would make a temporary residence near Mary's possible family a more focused hypothesis; it would not prove a move, tenancy or inheritance.

The supplied extract also lists Robert Elder of **Gortaragh**, Arthur O'Neil of Tehorney, Henry and James Wallace of Culmore, James Tomb of Ballymaconly and James Elder of Drumcon. Their combined names and literal place spellings are useful for locating the correct column despite imperfect OCR. They must not yet be treated as neighbours, fellow freeholders or relatives. The 1829 Robert Elder cannot comfortably be the later son-in-law whose [1871 marriage](https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/marriage_returns/marriages_1871/11341/8162804.pdf) gives age forty and father Nathaniel; the corresponding [1894 death](https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/deaths_returns/deaths_1894/05952/4691448.pdf) gives age sixty-four. Those dates place that Robert's birth around 1830–31. A different Elder generation is therefore the appropriate comparison, and **Gortaragh** is left unnormalised pending the page.

The next test is the full image of page 4 and the heading governing this entry, with adjoining columns. The earlier PRONI freeholder-search negative does not dispose of this newspaper occurrence. The surname-search failure is now demonstrably an OCR limitation: the exact townland retrieves article 015. Neither search outcomes nor damaged heading text determine the qualification or age of the named man.

### What the land records can establish

Alexander could have been the 1834 occupier at about twenty-three. An older namesake remains possible, but the name alone does not require one. In the 1836 field book, the house section names Robert Glasgow and Archibald McCaughan junior; the land section supplies no occupier names. Alexander’s omission cannot prove he held no land, lived with Robert, or had not yet formed a household.

### The farm and the Elder connection

| Lisnagaver lot | Occupier | Area in valuation | Immediate lessor |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 24 | [John Glasgow](/people/glasgow-867.html) | 21 acres, 2 roods, 25 perches | Robert Harvey |
| 25 | Alexander Glasgow | 8 acres, 2 roods, 10 perches | Robert Harvey |
| 26a | [Thomas Glasgow](/people/glasgow-987.html) | 32 acres, 3 roods, 15 perches | Robert Harvey |

Source: General Valuation of Ireland and [PRONI valuation revision books](https://apps.proni.gov.uk/Val12B/Search.aspx), Lisnagaver, VAL/12/B/4/16A–D. The 1834 tithe’s Plantation acreage and the valuation’s statute acreage cannot be directly equated to reconstruct an inheritance. The earlier near-equality argument is superseded. Adjoining holdings do not establish three brothers or a particular father.

Robert Elder’s succession to the **same numbered holding** is more specific than two surname occurrences in one parish. It supports continuity between Alexander’s family and his daughter’s husband. The immediate lessor was Robert Harvey: this is an estate tenancy, not evidence of freehold ownership. Neither succession nor the annotated revision years prove inheritance or an exact death date. The independent civil records that carry the Elder family to Gortahar are set out once, in the [death-identification chain](#death-assessment).

The later [1901](https://nationalarchives.ie/collections/search-the-census/census-record/#id=4575739&c20_year=1901) and [1911](https://nationalarchives.ie/collections/search-the-census/census-record/#id=490671&c20_year=1911) Gortahar Elder households are supporting family continuations, **not censuses of Alexander**. Their contribution to Alexander’s family account is explained [above](#children-adults); complete household details remain on [Mary’s page](/people/glasgow-3167.html).

biography_sections.title: Testing the 1888 death identification
biography_sections.markdown:
**The death at Gortahar on 16 May 1888 remains the best-supported located match for [Alexander Glasgow of Lisnagaver (Glasgow-951)](/people/glasgow-951.html), but its identification is probable rather than uniquely proved.** The case rests on a connected family and landholding sequence. The register supplies an exact death date; uncertainty concerns the deceased’s identity, not the precision of that date.

### The record and its limits

[Original death entry 348](https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/deaths_returns/deaths_1888/06179/4766466.pdf) supplies the following details. Nancy’s age and marital status are not recorded; no wife, parent, birthplace or former Lisnagaver address identifies the deceased more narrowly.

### The register at a glance

| Field | Entry 348 |
| --- | --- |
| Registration | Dirraw registrar’s district, Ballymoney union, County Antrim |
| Death | 16 May 1888, Gortahar |
| Name and status | Alexander Glasgow; male; married |
| Age and occupation | 84 years; labourer |
| Cause | Gangrene, three months, certified |
| Informant | Nancy Glasgow, her mark; daughter; present at death; **Gortahar** |
| Registration date | 25 May 1888 |

{{record:alex1888-death}}

{{record:alex1888-informant}}

### The identity chain, in dependency order

1. The [1851 Lisnagaver house-35 return](https://nationalarchives.ie/collections/search-the-census/view-pdf/?doc=007246523_00175&c19=true) establishes Alexander and wife Mary, both reported aged 40, with children Robert, James and Ann. This is the starting household; its identity does not depend on either Gortahar death.
2. [Mary Glasgow’s 14 June 1871 marriage](https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/marriage_returns/marriages_1871/11341/8162804.pdf) identifies a 28-year-old Lisnagaver spinster, daughter of Alexander Glasgow, farmer, marrying Robert Elder, 40, farmer of Gortereghy. It directly establishes the bride’s father. Linking that father to the established Lisnagaver household uses name, residence and occupation; the marriage does not name her mother.
3. [PRONI valuation revisions](https://apps.proni.gov.uk/Val12B/Search.aspx), VAL/12/B/4/16C–D, follow Alexander’s removal from **Lisnagaver lot 25** and Robert Elder’s subsequent occupation. Succession to the particular holding strengthens the identification of Robert with the daughter’s husband. The book neither declares an inheritance nor records Alexander’s destination or exact death. It supplies a separate administrative connection, not another explicit statement of kinship.
4. The [16 September 1878 birth of Jane Matilda Elder](https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/birth_returns/births_1878/02945/2078820.pdf) places Robert Elder and Mary, maiden surname **Glass**, at Gortahar. The spelling is retained as written. The parents and later household continuity support identification with the 1871 couple; the shortened surname alone would be insufficient.
5. [Mary Glasgow’s death on 17 February 1892](https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/deaths_returns/deaths_1892/06049/4723532.pdf), entry 234, records a widow aged 89 at Gortahar, with **daughter Mary Elder** present. That named relationship supplies the strongest connection between the elderly Glasgow woman and the Elder family. With the preceding marriage and household evidence, it supports the high-confidence identification of the widow as [Mary McCaughan (McCaughan-222)](/people/mccaughan-222.html). It does **not** name her deceased husband.
6. The 1888 death of a married Alexander Glasgow in the same townland fits the husband of that widow. This last step remains inferential: neither death expressly identifies the other deceased as spouse, and Nancy has not yet been connected independently to the Lisnagaver family.

The [1901](https://nationalarchives.ie/collections/search-the-census/census-record/#id=4575739&c20_year=1901) and [1911](https://nationalarchives.ie/collections/search-the-census/census-record/#id=490671&c20_year=1911) Elder households strengthen the family continuation. They are not independent sightings of Alexander. Likewise, the two civil deaths cannot first be assumed to concern a married couple and then cited as independent proof of that assumption. Their combined value depends on the independently established Elder connection.

### Ages and occupation: compatibility with genuine conflicts

| Person | 1851 reported age | Later death age | Approximate discrepancy |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Alexander | 40, implying c.1811 | 84 in 1888, implying c.1804 | Seven years older than expected |
| Mary | 40, implying c.1811 | 89 in 1892, implying c.1803 | Eight years older than expected |

The two death ages describe near-contemporary people, as does the census, and both imply births several years earlier. This parallel is compatible with one elderly couple whose ages were reported differently across records. It does not prove shared identity: the informants may have had incomplete knowledge, the census ages may be inaccurate, or a namesake could be involved. Neither age should silently replace the maintained approximate birth estimate. The paired pattern becomes relevant only after the family connection has been established.

Alexander’s change from farmer to labourer is less problematic. [Ann Glasgow’s 13 October 1876 marriage to Robert McCracken](https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/marriage_returns/marriages_1876/11181/8097170.pdf) already calls her father Alexander a labourer. Thus the 1888 occupation is compatible with the known father twelve years earlier; it does not require a different man. Conversely, labourer is too common an occupation to identify him by itself.

### Nancy and the competing Alexander

[Nancy’s possible identification with Ann (Glasgow-438)](/people/glasgow-438.html) remains open. Ann had married in 1876 and would ordinarily appear as McCracken. No inspected record calls her Nancy or places her at Gortahar in 1888. Use of Glasgow does not establish that Nancy was unmarried, but it is a real obstacle to equating the two. Another daughter, absent in 1851 or born later, remains possible; no such birth or relationship should be invented.

[Alexander of Glenleslie (Glasgow-2385)](/people/glasgow-2385.html) is a genuine competing labourer. His [1847 marriage to Mary Anne Martin](https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/marriage_returns/marriages_1847/09322/5375567.pdf) and [1851 household](https://nationalarchives.ie/collections/search-the-census/census-record/#id=32216&census_year=1851) distinguish a coherent family with wife Mary Ann and son John. A reported age of 35 in 1851 implies about 72 in 1888, twelve years below the death age. No located record connects this household to Nancy, Gortahar or the Elder succession. He is weaker, not excluded.

The reported 1882 death of his wife is **unverified**. Her current [WikiTree biography](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Martin-93219), checked through the live API, supplies no identifiable original death registration and includes an 1848 Sydney marriage description concerning Mary Ann Cupid. That material cannot establish the Irish wife’s death. Even a verified death would require checking remarriage before using the 1888 married status to exclude her husband.

### Comparing the named candidates

| Candidate | Fit to the Gortahar death | Present assessment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Alexander of Lisnagaver, Glasgow-951 | Known family reaches Gortahar; father described as labourer by 1876; widow and daughter fit the Elder network | **Best current fit; probable.** Age and Nancy’s identity remain unresolved. |
| [Alexander of Glenleslie (Glasgow-2385)](/people/glasgow-2385.html), born about 1816; husband of Mary Anne Martin | A real Antrim labourer namesake. He would have been about 72, a worse age fit to 84. No located Gortahar, Nancy or Elder connection identifies him with the death | **Weaker alternative, not conclusively excluded.** Trace his later household and wife independently before any reassignment. |
| [Older Alexander (Glasgow-3904)](/people/glasgow-3904.html), estimated birth c.1770 in the parent tradition | Would have been about 118 in 1888; neither the reported generation nor family history fits | **No plausible claim on present chronology.** His own estimated identity is not an original death identification. |

Thomas’s daughter [Nancy Glasgow (Glasgow-1362)](/people/glasgow-1362.html) is another local name, but the death expressly calls its informant Alexander’s daughter. Substituting Thomas’s daughter would require a relationship error or further evidence; she is not an equally straightforward identification.

The old 22 May 1852 death belongs to an unsupported Australian reconstruction of a different family. The submitted DNA-project ancestor label repeating “d.1852” is not a death record.

### What would change the conclusion?

A record linking Nancy to Alexander and Mary of Lisnagaver, or a burial or notice naming the Gortahar man’s wife or former residence, would strengthen the leading identification. A securely identified death of Alexander-951 elsewhere, or an independently documented Glenleslie-to-Gortahar household with daughter Nancy, would challenge it. Tracing the Glenleslie son’s reported 1870 marriage offers a specific next step toward later family residence; that profile-derived lead still needs its original. Present evidence supports retaining **16 May 1888, Gortahar, probable identification**, with the identity chain and its dependencies visible.

Original excerpts shown here were checked against the saved images. The Mary–Robert Elder 1871 marriage and Mary Glasgow 1892 death remain linked above and supported by the earlier maintained readings; fresh image retrieval returned an access error during this illustration pass, so no new excerpt or fresh reading is claimed for them.

reading_summary.question: Is the 1888 Gortahar death Alexander’s?
reading_summary.finding: It is the best-supported located match, but age conflict and Nancy’s unresolved identity prevent unique proof.
reading_summary.purpose: Weighs the full identity chain and competing candidates.

biography_sections.title: Y-DNA: the connection and the competing histories
biography_sections.markdown:
[Alexander Glasgow (Glasgow-951)](/people/glasgow-951.html) is the project owner’s **oldest confirmed direct paternal ancestor**. The documented descent reaches Alexander; his parents remain unknown. A tested male-line descendant has **Big Y-700 placement R-FT20271**, also found in a tested descendant of [James J Glasgow (Glasgow-2738)](/people/glasgow-2738.html), born about 1809–10. These are historical ancestors represented by descendant results, not people who were themselves tested. The shared branch establishes paternal genetic kinship between the tested lines. It does not extend either documentary pedigree automatically. [FamilyTreeDNA Glasgow project results](https://www.familytreedna.com/public/Glasgow?iframe=ydna-results-overview), checked 13 September 2026.

This gives the parentage investigation a concrete family network. Alexander’s connection to James J’s line is established genetically even though the bridge between their families is missing. James J’s proposed father [Robert Glasgow (Glasgow-2769)](/people/glasgow-2769.html) and proposed earlier connection to [Archibald Glasgow (Glasgow-2304)](/people/glasgow-2304.html) remain hypotheses. Inserting them into a proved descent would assume the answer. See [James J’s evidence and open parentage question](/people/glasgow-2738.html).

### What close STR matching can tell us

The maintained comparison gives **genetic distance three at Y-111** between the Alexander and James J descendant lines. That makes their connection a valuable research priority. It does not mean three generations: STR changes accumulate unevenly, and observed distance is not the number of father-to-son transmissions. [FTDNA’s explanation of genetic distance](https://blog.familytreedna.com/ftdnatip-report/).

Another Glasgow line is closer on the larger callable Big Y STR comparison. Consequently James J is the nearest comparison on the specified Y-111 panel, not demonstrably Alexander’s nearest genealogical cousin. The inspected August 2026 Block Tree contains no exclusive named downstream branch joining only these two lines. [Wider Y-DNA study and comparison evidence](/ydna/).

Brothers, paternal cousins and descendants of more distant collateral branches remain distinguishable historical hypotheses; the present DNA cannot choose among them. Their similar estimated birth years do not locate their common ancestor. A connection through an earlier generation, followed by migration in one branch, remains compatible with the results. A specific migration route is not established. An exact ancestor, date or cousin degree requires evidence connecting the named people, supported where possible by additional independent descendant comparisons.

{{figure:paternal-branches.svg}}

### The SNP evidence matrix

The abbreviated branch path is **R-FT4811 → R-FT32941 → R-FT25406 → R-FT20271**, with FTE32242 downstream. Historical names below label descendant lines, not tested historical people.

**State key:** **D** = derived, the changed state; **A** = ancestral, the pre-mutation state supported by a direct call; **U** = unresolved in the reviewed evidence; **UT** = untested at SNP level in the supplied comparison. A **no-call** means an attempted call was inconclusive and remains unresolved. **Not independently reviewed** describes the evidence or pedigree audit, not a genotype. No row is labelled no-call without evidence of an actual no-call.

| Historical paternal line | FT20271 | FT6135 | FTE32242 | Provenance and pedigree qualification |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Alexander Glasgow (Glasgow-951)](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Glasgow-951) | **D**: direct audit and public placement | **A**: direct reliable call | **U**: basal display is insufficient to prove ancestral | Public project, 13 Sep 2026; private call audit, 11 Aug 2026. Established descendant line in this case; Alexander's parents remain unknown. |
| [James J Glasgow (Glasgow-2738)](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Glasgow-2738) | **D**: public placement | **U**: direct state not independently reviewed | **U**: basal display only | Public project, 13 Sep 2026; Aug administrator mapping. Descent to James J is distinguished from his uncertain attachment to Robert-2769 and Archibald-2304. |
| Reported [William Glasgow (Glasgow-591)](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Glasgow-591), c.1655 | **D**: reported public placement | **U** | **U**: basal display only | Aug 2026 project evidence; early pedigree not independently established here. |
| Reported [Robert Glasgow (Glasgow-12)](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Glasgow-12), through [John M (Glasgow-1965)](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Glasgow-1965) | **D**: reported public placement | **D**: supplied comparison | **U**: basal display only | Aug call comparison; maintained Y-DNA study maps this result through John M with a probable private continuation. This is a reported son-line of Robert, not an independently verified earlier root. |
| Reported Robert Glasgow, through [William (Glasgow-563)](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Glasgow-563) | **D**: reported public placement | **D**: supplied comparison | **U**: basal display only | Aug call comparison; the maintained pedigree audit identifies William’s line. The older James c.1700 ancestor label is not an independent test of Robert’s father or grandfather. |
| [James M Glasgow (Glasgow-193)](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Glasgow-193), through [William Allen (Glasgow-2182)](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Glasgow-2182) | **D**: upstream of displayed child | **U**: direct call required | **D**: public child-branch association | Aug 2026 project and Block Tree evidence; historical association conditional on the supplied father-to-son pedigree. |
| James M Glasgow, through [Samuel Lyle (Glasgow-192)](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Glasgow-192) | **D**: upstream of displayed child | **U**: direct call required | **D**: public child-branch association | Same dated evidence; independently documented descent still needs checking at the relevant joining generations. |
| Reported [Robert Glasgow of Kilwaughter (Glasgow-1143)](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Glasgow-1143) | **UT** | **UT** | **UT** | Aug 2026 Y-111 comparison only. The ancestor label is a candidate identification; STR grouping does not establish FT20271 membership. |
| Reported [James of Kilwaughter, later South Carolina (Glasgow-1144)](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Glasgow-1144) | **UT** | **UT** | **UT** | Maintained historical mapping and Y-37 comparison, reviewed 13 Sep 2026. Public broad haplogroup/STR grouping does not establish FT20271. Audit the descendant path before assigning its result to this ancestor. |
| Reported [John of Inishrush, later Ohio (Glasgow-822)](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Glasgow-822) | **UT** | **UT** | **UT** | Maintained historical mapping and Y-67 comparison, reviewed 13 Sep 2026. Public broad haplogroup/STR grouping does not establish FT20271. Audit the descendant path before assigning its result to this ancestor. |

Public source: [FamilyTreeDNA Glasgow project](https://www.familytreedna.com/public/Glasgow?iframe=ydna-results-overview). Safe study context: [Y-DNA research](/ydna/). Private-call results above are a summary of the maintained August audit, not an independently reproducible public genotype dataset.

The maintained pedigree audit places the two FT6135 comparison results through Robert’s sons William and John M, with different confidence in their later continuations. The older James c.1700 label must not be counted as an independent test above Robert.

The FT6135 difference is real in the audited Alexander result and the two supplied comparison results. Its position outside the currently accepted child-branch display makes it a **candidate grouping signal**, not an established new branch. Resolve FT6135 in both James M son-lines first: derived results would support inheritance at or above Robert under the reported pedigrees and a simple inheritance model; ancestral results would contradict that simple model and require checking pedigrees, recurrence or reversion. Inadequate coverage would leave the issue open. Neither outcome alone identifies Alexander's father.

The two FTE32242-positive son-lines associate that branch with James M's descendants, conditionally on their pedigrees. To locate it below Robert generally requires a reliable ancestral result in a separately documented Robert line. A basal FT20271 label supplies no such result. Missing entries in a variants-only file likewise do not prove ancestral states. [FTDNA SNP and match guidance](https://help.familytreedna.com/hc/en-us/articles/4402696079887-Big-Y-Matching-Matches-Guide).

For Alexander and James J, compare existing consented calls at named and private variants with coverage and pedigree checks. A shared additional derived state could refine their genetic grouping; it would not make the historical men brothers or identify the mutation's generation. A separately documented Alexander son-line could distinguish variants inherited through Alexander or earlier from changes arising later in one descendant line. STR distance and rounded private-variant averages reuse existing observations: they do not independently date the common ancestor. No narrow common-ancestor date is justified here.


One Robert-associated line and one James M descendant are identical at Y-111 despite different displayed SNP branches. STR similarity therefore cannot recover every branching event. The previous STR reconstruction’s approximate 1750 horizon also reuses marker evidence and has unconstrained dates conflicting with known genealogy; it is not an independent historical date.

The table is available as [CSV](/assets/research/glasgow-951-dna-matrix.csv) and [JSON](/assets/research/glasgow-951-dna-matrix.json), with its dated provenance and unresolved states. A public branch placement can be rechecked at the project; the private-call summary requires the underlying consented files for replication.


The [Larne reconstruction](#larne-reconstruction) connects these genetic comparisons to the actual American and Irish family hypotheses, with each missing generation assessed separately.
